strengths: Novel algorithmic contribution: RSPG is the first history-aware HSM for POMFGs-CN, extending prior work (SPG) from memoryless to recurrent policies in a non-trivial way

Clever tractability insight: The 'shared observations' special case elegantly avoids exponential blowup in observation history tracking, well-motivated for realistic applications with public information

Strong empirical validation: Consistent lowest/second-lowest exploitability across three environments, order-of-magnitude speedup over RL methods in wall-clock time, qualitative analysis demonstrating learned anticipatory behavior

Significant practical contribution: MFAX framework addresses genuine gaps (10-1000× faster mean-field updates, supports partial observability/common noise/white-box dynamics distinction), publicly released for community use
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, multi-seed experiments with confidence intervals, comprehensive ablations (ordinal vs categorical policies), algorithm code released
Useful conceptual contribution: Unified taxonomy of DP/RL/HSMs in Section 3 clarifies fragmented MFG literature
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical analysis: No convergence guarantees, no formal justification for policy restriction to π(·|st, o0:t) maintaining optimality, stop-gradient operations in Algorithm 1 are crucial but only informally justified

Restrictive problem assumptions: Requires white-box transition dynamics (limits applicability when dynamics unknown), assumes shared observations (may not hold with heterogeneous information), only finite-horizon problems tested, limited to discrete/discretizable state spaces

Limited experimental scope: Only 3 environments, 2 toy problems, largest experiment uses 1000 discrete states; no demonstration of scalability to realistic problem sizes, missing comparison with Yongacoglu et al. (2024) on partially observable MFGs

Unfair algorithm comparison: Asymmetric hyperparameter search effort (3 for RSPG vs 81 for IPPO/RIPPO vs 243 for M-OMD) raises fairness concerns; SPG achieves similar exploitability to RSPG on macroeconomics suggesting history may not be essential

Exploitability metric concerns: Using perfect information best-response creates loose upper bound on equilibrium distance; differs from standard Nash exploitability, making absolute values less interpretable

Insufficient technical justification: Footnote 3's claim about stochastic observations being WLOG needs expansion; Equation (11) mixing observation generation with trajectory tracking could be clearer; observation history o0:t still grows linearly with time, unclear where tractability gain vs full IAOH tracking is concretely achieved
Dense presentation: 24 main pages + 26 appendix with key specs relegated to appendix; notation could streamline (μ̃ vs μ, τ for history); architecture diagram appears late

Missing analyses: No ablation on effective history length, sensitivity to observation quality, RNN dimensionality effects; no empirical convergence curves (exploitability vs iteration); no analysis of discretization bias in macroeconomics environment

strengths: Cleanly identifies and solves the tractability problem for history-dependent policies in partially observable MFGs through shared observations restriction, enabling practical algorithms that combine HSMs with recurrence

MFAX framework makes genuine engineering contributions: 10-1000× speedup through functional mean-field updates, cleaner white-box/black-box distinction, supports features (partial observability, common noise, multiple µ₀) absent from OpenSpiel/MFGLib

Thorough empirical work with careful ablations, qualitative analysis showing learned anticipatory behaviors (Beach Bar closure prediction, macroeconomic spending patterns), extensive implementation details, and promised code release
Clear mathematical formulation of POMFGs-CN and the shared observation restriction; well-motivated by economic applications (market prices as common observations)
Solves first macroeconomics MFG instance with heterogeneous agents, common noise, and history-aware policies
weaknesses: Scope of partial observability severely overstated: restriction to shared observations (ot = U(µt, zt), no individual state dependence) is fundamental and very limiting, yet presented as a minor technical detail; essentially solves 'public information games' not general POMFGs

Algorithmic novelty is incremental: RSPG = Yang et al. (2025) SPG + RNN with no new theoretical machinery, convergence guarantees, or sample complexity analysis; straightforward application of known techniques

Weak evidence that history actually helps: Linear Quadratic shows SPG ≈ RSPG exploitability despite finite horizon where history should matter; Macroeconomics shows identical exploitability (Figure 2) with history benefits only qualitative; missing ablation on history truncation length

Unfair experimental comparison: HSMs' speedup comes primarily from analytical mean-field updates (known advantage independent of RSPG), not algorithmic novelty; different hyperparameter sweep counts (3 vs 81 vs 243) across algorithms; wall-clock comparison obscures fundamental differences in variance vs sample complexity

Small-scale experiments (|S| ≤ 1000, mostly ≤ 100; |A| ≤ 20) with unclear scaling; unclear how discretization choices affect macroeconomics results; no evaluation on larger problems where history tractability matters more

Algorithm design choices under-justified: stop-gradient through mean-field updates limits policy influence on future states (not discussed as limitation); no ablation on RNN architecture choice; policy architecture constraints (hidden state independent of s_t) necessary for tractability but flexibility lost

Exploitability metric uses best-response over more expressive policy class than learned class, making zero exploitability unattainable and convergence interpretation ambiguous; unusual choice not standard in literature

Presentation obscures limitations: title/abstract claim 'Partially Observable MFGs' when actually requires shared observations; 'state-of-the-art' claimed without clear baseline; 'order-of-magnitude faster' comes from JAX/GPU engineering + analytical updates, not RSPG; key restriction buried in Section 5.1
Paper tries to do too much (algorithm + framework + taxonomy + problem formulation), diluting focus; theoretical contributions entirely absent despite space devoted to DP/RL/HSM taxonomy

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Identifies shared observations as a tractable special case of POMFGs-CN, enabling history-dependent policies while preserving computational tractability - clever theoretical insight
First history-aware HSM: RSPG extends hybrid structural methods to partial observability, a previously unexplored direction with clear practical benefits
Strong empirical results: Achieves order-of-magnitude faster convergence than RL baselines across all three environments while maintaining or improving exploitability
High-quality software contribution: MFAX achieves 10-1000× speedups through functional matrix-vector representations and clean architectural design (white-box/black-box separation)
Comprehensive reproducibility: Detailed pseudocode, hyperparameter sweeps (243 configurations for M-OMD), network architectures, and promised code release
Excellent pedagogical contribution: Section 3's unified taxonomy of DP/RL/HSM approaches clearly delineates assumptions and is missing from MFG literature
Realistic application: First successful application to Krusell-Smith macroeconomics model with partial observability and common noise, demonstrating practical relevance
Qualitative analysis: Figures 3-4 effectively demonstrate that history-dependent policies learn meaningful anticipatory behavior (e.g., agents moving before bar closes)
Well-written: Clear structure, good motivation, effective use of information boxes, comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: No convergence theory: Lacks formal convergence guarantees or even empirical convergence rate analysis. While practical assumptions often fail, some theoretical grounding would strengthen the work

Restrictive key assumption: Shared observations (o_t = U(µ_t, z_t)) fundamentally limits scope - excludes settings where observations depend on individual state. Limited discussion of robustness when violated
Limited experimental scope: Only 3 environments (2 toy problems with 100 states; 1 specialized finite-horizon macroeconomic model). No stress tests on state/action scalability or generalization

Insufficient design choice justification: (1) Why stop gradients through mean-field updates but allow them through transitions? (2) Why is policy architecture (hidden state independent of individual state) optimal? (3) No ablations for structured prior on continuous actions except one figure
Conservative exploitability metric: Computing over perfect information best-response policies provides upper bound, making zero exploitability unachievable. Implications inadequately discussed
Missing key comparisons: No direct comparison to Benjamin & Abate (2025), which addresses similar partial observability setting. Limited baseline comparisons overall
Narrow problem scope: Requires either (a) known transition dynamics and finite state/action spaces, or (b) acceptable discretization. Specialized to academic settings
Modest differences in some cases: Macroeconomics environment shows SPG and RSPG achieving similar exploitability (Figure 2), despite qualitative behavioral differences (Figure 3). Gap unexplained
Limited robustness analysis: No evaluation of sensitivity to observation noise, state space size, common noise intensity, or history length
Incomplete practical guidance: How to choose observation function U in practice? When does shared observation assumption approximately hold? Memory requirements for large |S|?

strengths: Addresses important gap by extending HSMs to partially observable settings with history-dependent policies
Elegant technical insight that restricting memory to public observation history avoids exponential history space blow-up while maintaining tractability
Comprehensive experimental methodology with fair comparisons, extensive hyperparameter sweeps (81-243 configs), and proper reproducibility practices
Demonstrates order-of-magnitude (~10×) faster convergence than model-free RL methods while learning realistic behaviors
Valuable engineering contribution: MFAX framework with 10-1000× speedups over existing libraries through functional matrix representations
Clear presentation of DP/RL/HSM taxonomy provides pedagogical value
Excellent visualization of learned behaviors showing anticipatory actions in Beach Bar and Macroeconomics environments
weaknesses: Core Assumption 6.1 (sufficient public partial information) lacks rigorous justification; Appendix A counter-example shows it can be violated; limited evidence for claimed broad applicability
No convergence guarantees to MFG Nash equilibrium; empirical stability insufficient for top-tier venue; authors acknowledge theoretical barriers but don't resolve them
Limited experimental scope: only 3 environments with small state/action spaces (|S|≤1000); Beach Bar shows RSPG sometimes matches memoryless SPG contradicting benefits-of-memory claims
Incomplete technical details: mean-field update computation (Eqs. 11-13) still requires intractable integration; practical handling of individual-state-dependent observations unspecified
Missing analysis: no characterization of approximation error from Assumption 6.1, no sample complexity bounds, no sensitivity analysis on recurrent capacity
Evaluation uses larger perfect-information policy class for fairness to memoryless methods; conservative but potentially masks issues; confidence intervals in Figure 2 are wide
Theoretical novelty is incremental: adding a GRU to SPG is straightforward; restricting to public observation history is intuitive but perhaps obvious in retrospect

strengths: Clear presentation with useful taxonomy (Section 4) organizing DP, RL, and HSM methods for MFGs
MFAX framework provides genuine practical value with 10-1000× speedup over existing libraries and thoughtful engineering (functional matrix-vector products, GPU parallelization)
Careful formalization of POMFGs-CN in Section 5 and of the restricted policy class under Assumptions 1.1 and 6.1
Good reproducibility: promised code release, extensive hyperparameter details, pseudocode, and full environment specifications in appendices
Effective visualizations (Figures 3, 4, 8) demonstrating that learned policies capture anticipatory behavior missed by memoryless methods
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is adding a GRU to encode shared observations and conditioning policy on (st, o0:t). This is a straightforward application of RNN-based POMDP policies, not a novel algorithmic insight

Critical Assumption 6.1 (Sufficient Public Partial Information) is foundational but unjustified: (a) a counter-example violating the assumption is provided in Appendix A and acknowledged; (b) assumption is presented as 'useful approximation' without specifying scope or conditions; (c) zero empirical validation of robustness when assumption is violated

Insufficient experimental validation: only 3 environments tested (2 toy problems with |S| ≤ 100); all appear artificially constructed to satisfy Assumption 6.1; no experiments comparing performance on environments where assumption holds vs. fails; Figure 2 shows SPG and RSPG converge to similar exploitability in Macroeconomics, undercutting claims of consistent improvement

Unfair evaluation metric: uses perfect-information policy class ΠPI rather than admissible class Πeval, systematically disadvantaging memoryless methods. Authors acknowledge XΠ_PI is 'regret-like upper bound rather than exact distance to equilibrium' but proceed anyway without also reporting true Nash distance

No convergence guarantees despite claims of improved efficiency: paper provides no theoretical analysis or rates; prior work (Yongacoglu et al. 2024) guarantees convergence for memoryless policies in similar settings but RSPG extends to history-dependent case without such guarantees

Unjustified technical choices: (1) stop-gradient applied to mean-field updates (Algorithm 1) without justification or impact analysis; (2) continuous action discretization on fixed grids lacks sensitivity analysis despite Section D.4.1 showing importance; (3) variance reduction claims overstated since HSMs still sample common noise

Missing comparisons: no experiments against belief-state methods, filtering approaches, or modern POMDP techniques; related work on Subramanian et al. (2020) and Benjamin & Abate (2025) mentioned but not empirically compared

Scalability undemonstrated: claims HSMs 'scale poorly' but doesn't prove RSPG scales; largest tested environment has |S|=1000 (discretized); no wall-clock comparison vs. state-of-the-art on same computational budget

strengths: Novel combination: First work to simultaneously address common noise, partial observability, and history-dependent policies in Hybrid Structural Methods
Elegant technical insight: Assumption 6.1 cleverly enables history-awareness while maintaining computational tractability by restricting to public observation history
Solid technical execution: Rigorous problem formulation, correct derivation of analytic mean-field updates, clear algorithms
Strong empirical results: Order-of-magnitude speedups over model-free RL methods (IPPO, RIPPO, M-OMD) with convincing visualizations of learned anticipatory behavior
Valuable infrastructure: MFAX framework provides 10-1000× speedup over existing libraries with clean white-box/black-box separation
Good experimental methodology: Fair comparison using wall-clock time, multiple relevant baselines, detailed hyperparameters provided for reproducibility
Clear presentation: Well-written with pedagogical information boxes; comprehensive appendices with full specifications enable reproducibility
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical guarantees: No convergence analysis to MFG Nash equilibrium; authors acknowledge extending existing guarantees is non-trivial due to violations of standard assumptions

Restrictive Assumption 6.1: The assumption that p(µt, zt | τt) = p(µt, zt | st, o0:t) can be violated (counter-example in Appendix A shows 2× reward gap), but no empirical evaluation on environments where assumption is nearly violated
Limited experimental scope: Only 3 environments with small state spaces (100-1000 discrete states); no evaluation on truly large-scale problems or study of computational scaling with |S|, |A|
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Misses comparison to Benjamin & Abate (2025) and Yongacoglu et al. (2024) on partially observable MFGs; unclear when RSPG dominates alternatives

Evaluation metric concerns: Uses perfect-information policy class for exploitability evaluation, making it a 'conservative regret-like upper bound' rather than true Nash distance; gap between this and admissible class not quantified
Design choices lack justification: Continuous action discretization appears ad-hoc; GRU hidden size (64) unused without ablation; no sensitivity analysis for observation function design or noise
Incomplete ablations: Only policy parameterization ablated; missing ablations on GRU size, number of environments, architecture choices, and most importantly sensitivity to Assumption 6.1 violations

Overlapping results in some cases: Macroeconomics shows SPG and RSPG achieve nearly identical exploitability (Figure 2), weakening the case for RSPG beyond behavioral differences; large confidence intervals in Beach Bar results
